questions.title: How does the substantial evidence standard work when reviewing BIA findings of fact in asylum cases?
questions.question_body: In Jimenez v. Bondi, the court says it reviews the BIA's findings of fact under a "substantial-evidence standard" and that findings are "conclusive unless the record demonstrates that any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary." I'm confused about how deferential this really is in practice. The court seems to go through the evidence and agree with the BIA at every step, but how is this different from de novo review? At what point would a court actually find that the evidence "compels" a contrary conclusion? Is there a meaningful difference between substantial evidence review and just deferring to whatever the agency decided?

questions.title: Can threats and psychological harm ever constitute persecution, or is physical harm always required?
questions.question_body: The court in Jimenez v. Bondi says that "threats alone are insufficient to constitute persecution" and that it has "rarely, if ever, granted asylum based on threats and emotional or psychological harm alone." But the court also says physical harm is "not necessary" to satisfy the persecution prong and that incidents should be considered "collectively" for their cumulative effect. The petitioners here received death threats, were held at gunpoint, had an employee assaulted, and had a man grab their child at school. If all of that combined doesn't rise to persecution, what would? Is there any Tenth Circuit case where non-physical harm alone was found to constitute persecution? I'm having trouble understanding where the line actually is.

questions.title: How does the "at least one central reason" nexus test work in mixed-motive persecution cases?
questions.question_body: In Jimenez v. Bondi, the court discusses mixed motives—the persecutor can have multiple reasons for targeting someone, but the protected ground must be "at least one central reason." Here, the petitioners were politically active AND Jimenez interfered with Don Rafa's property/criminal operations. The court found the political opinion was "tangential and subordinate" to the property dispute. But what if the persecutor was motivated 40% by political opinion and 60% by the personal dispute—is that enough for nexus? How do courts actually weigh or rank motives to determine if a protected ground is "central" versus "incidental"? Is there a threshold percentage or is it purely qualitative?

questions.title: What counts as sufficient reporting to police for the "unable or unwilling" government protection analysis?
questions.question_body: The court in Jimenez v. Bondi emphasizes that reporting past persecution to the government is "a key fact" in the unable-or-unwilling analysis. The petitioners spoke to two individual police officers who told them to leave, but the court said this was insufficient because it doesn't show the "Colombian government's position"—just individual officer apathy. The court also notes the petitioners didn't report through Jimenez's law enforcement contacts or outside their neighborhood. So my question is: how much reporting is enough? Do you need to file formal police reports, escalate to higher authorities, or try multiple precincts? At what point does individual officer failure become evidence of systemic government inability or unwillingness? The court says a "one-off conversation" isn't enough, but how many conversations would be?

questions.title: How does the futility exception work when an applicant claims reporting to police would be dangerous?
questions.question_body: In Jimenez v. Bondi, the court says an applicant can satisfy the government protection requirement by showing that filing a police report would have been "futile or dangerous." The petitioners argued that contacting the government would be futile because their persecutors are aligned with the president of Colombia. But the court rejected this because the government had actually attempted searches and seizures at Don Rafa's property. I'm confused about what evidence is needed to prove futility. If the persecutor is allegedly connected to the government, does the applicant need to prove that every possible avenue of protection would fail? Does evidence of some government enforcement action against the persecutor automatically defeat a futility claim?

questions.title: Why does failing the asylum standard automatically mean failing withholding of removal?
questions.question_body: At the end of Jimenez v. Bondi, the court says that because petitioners fail to demonstrate a well-founded fear of persecution under asylum standards, "they necessarily fail to meet the higher standard for withholding of removal." I know withholding of removal has a higher burden of proof, but I'm confused about how the standards actually differ. Is it just the percentage of likelihood (more likely than not vs. reasonable possibility)? Are the elements (persecution, nexus, government protection) the same for both? If the elements are identical but just the burden is higher, why does the court even need to separately analyze withholding—couldn't it just say "higher standard, so automatically fails"? What's the practical difference between these two forms of relief?

questions.title: How does internal relocation factor into asylum analysis when the applicant hasn't established past persecution?
questions.question_body: In Jimenez v. Bondi, the court addresses safe internal relocation even though it already concluded the petitioners failed to establish past persecution or a well-founded fear of future persecution. The court says relocation is relevant because the government can rebut a "presumption of a well-founded fear" by showing the applicant could relocate. But if there's no presumption because there's no past persecution, why is the court analyzing relocation at all? Is the court just being thorough, or is internal relocation an independent requirement that applicants must disprove? Also, the court notes the persecutors told petitioners to leave the neighborhood, not the country—how much weight does the scope of the persecutor's threat carry in the relocation analysis?

questions.title: When a single BIA member affirms the IJ's decision, what exactly does the reviewing court look at?
questions.question_body: In Jimenez v. Bondi, the court notes that "a single member of the BIA affirmed the IJ's decision" and therefore the court reviews "the BIA's decision" but is "not precluded from consulting the IJ's more complete explanation of those same grounds." I'm confused about the procedural posture here. When a single BIA member issues a brief affirmance without opinion, does the reviewing court treat the IJ's reasoning as the BIA's reasoning? What if the BIA member affirmed on different grounds than the IJ? How do you know which decision is actually being reviewed—the IJ's, the BIA's, or both? Does it matter whether the BIA adopted the IJ's reasoning wholesale or just affirmed the result?
